title: Avoid SELECT * in Production Queries
description: SELECT * statements read all columns from tables, which can be inefficient when only specific columns are needed. This leads to increased I/O, memory usage, and network transfer, especially with wide tables containing many columns or large data types like strings and binary data.
before_example: SELECT * FROM sales_data WHERE region = 'US' AND date >= '2024-01-01'
after_example: SELECT customer_id, product_name, sales_amount, order_date FROM sales_data WHERE region = 'US' AND date >= '2024-01-01'
expected_improvement: 30-50% reduction in data transfer and memory usage
conditions: when table has many columns
when only specific columns are needed for analysis
when query processes large datasets

title: Use Partition Pruning for Large Tables
description: Partition pruning allows queries to skip reading entire partitions when filters match partition columns. This dramatically reduces the amount of data scanned and improves query performance, especially for time-series data partitioned by date.
before_example: SELECT * FROM event_logs WHERE user_id = '12345' AND event_type = 'click'
after_example: SELECT * FROM event_logs WHERE date = '2024-01-15' AND user_id = '12345' AND event_type = 'click'
conditions: when querying partitioned tables
when partition columns are available for filtering
when scanning time-series or date-based data

title: Optimize JOIN Order for Performance
description: Join order significantly impacts performance. Place the smallest table first in the join sequence, and use broadcast joins for small dimension tables. The Databricks optimizer can automatically optimize joins, but explicit hints can help with complex queries.
query_pattern: SELECT ... FROM large_table JOIN small_table ON ...
before_example: SELECT l.*, s.name FROM large_fact_table l JOIN small_dim_table s ON l.dim_id = s.id
after_example: SELECT /*+ BROADCAST(s) */ l.*, s.name FROM large_fact_table l JOIN small_dim_table s ON l.dim_id = s.id
conditions: when joining tables of significantly different sizes
when dimension tables are small enough for broadcast
when experiencing slow join performance

title: Cache Frequently Accessed Tables
description: Caching stores table data in memory for faster access on subsequent queries. This is particularly effective for reference data, dimension tables, or datasets that are accessed multiple times within a session or across multiple queries.
expected_improvement: 2-10x faster query execution for cached data
conditions: when table is accessed multiple times
when table is relatively small (fits in cluster memory)
when table data doesn't change frequently

title: Replace UNION with UNION ALL When Possible
description: UNION performs duplicate elimination which requires additional processing and memory. UNION ALL simply concatenates results without deduplication, making it much faster and less resource-intensive when duplicates are not a concern.
before_example: SELECT customer_id, order_date FROM orders_2023 UNION SELECT customer_id, order_date FROM orders_2024
after_example: SELECT customer_id, order_date FROM orders_2023 UNION ALL SELECT customer_id, order_date FROM orders_2024
expected_improvement: 15-30% reduction in execution time and DBU usage
conditions: when duplicate rows are acceptable in results
when you know the datasets don't have overlapping data
when processing large datasets with UNION operations

title: Add LIMIT Clauses to Exploratory Queries
description: Exploratory queries without LIMIT clauses can process entire datasets unnecessarily. Adding LIMIT significantly reduces execution time and cost, especially during development and data exploration phases.
before_example: SELECT * FROM transaction_logs ORDER BY timestamp DESC
after_example: SELECT * FROM transaction_logs ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 1000
expected_improvement: 50-90% reduction in data processed and execution time
conditions: when exploring data or developing queries
when full dataset results are not needed
when using ORDER BY without LIMIT

title: Pre-aggregate Data for Repeated Analytics
description: Instead of running the same aggregation queries repeatedly, create materialized views or pre-aggregated tables. This reduces computation costs and improves query performance for common analytical patterns.
query_pattern: SELECT date, SUM(...), COUNT(...) FROM large_table GROUP BY date
before_example:
-- This query runs daily and processes the entire fact table each time
SELECT DATE(order_timestamp) as order_date, SUM(amount) as daily_sales, COUNT(*) as order_count FROM orders GROUP BY DATE(order_timestamp)
after_example:
-- Create materialized view for daily aggregations
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_sales_summary AS SELECT DATE(order_timestamp) as order_date, SUM(amount) as daily_sales, COUNT(*) as order_count FROM orders GROUP BY DATE(order_timestamp);
-- Now use the pre-aggregated data
SELECT * FROM daily_sales_summary WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01'
expected_improvement: 60-80% reduction in compute costs for repeated queries
conditions: when running the same aggregation queries regularly
when source data doesn't change frequently
when aggregation results are used by multiple users or dashboards

title: Handle NULL Values Explicitly in Comparisons
description: NULL values in comparisons can cause unexpected results and query failures. Explicitly handling NULLs with IS NULL/IS NOT NULL or COALESCE functions ensures reliable query behavior and prevents runtime errors.
after_example: SELECT * FROM customers WHERE phone = '555-1234' OR (phone IS NULL AND '555-1234' IS NULL)
conditions: when columns may contain NULL values
when experiencing unexpected filtering results
when queries fail due to NULL comparisons
